title: Disagreement without hatred
hookLine: arguing for heaven's sake, even in politics
tomorrow: the Torah says 'surely rebuke.' so why do some sages say hush?

cards: A family group chat, dinnertime. An uncle posts an article, a cousin fires back, and by dessert two people have left the chat. Some fights are worth having, and some only burn.
Pirkei Avot sorts them. An argument for the sake of heaven will last; one that isn't, won't. Which is for heaven?
Hillel and Shammai. Which isn't? Korach and all his company.
Wait. In the Torah, Korach's revolt is against Moses. So why doesn't the Mishnah say Korach and Moses?

teach.h: MOSES WAS NEVER REALLY IN IT.
teach.b: Some readers answer: because Moses was never really in it. Korach's crowd only looked united against him. Underneath, each wanted the top spot, so the real fight was among themselves.
An argument like that can't last, because nobody in it wants the truth, only the win. Hillel and Shammai are the other picture.
The Talmud says their two schools argued for three years, until a voice from heaven said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. Why Hillel?
Because they were gentle and humble, they taught their own view and Shammai's too, and they even said Shammai's view first. And here's the line to tell a friend tonight.
The two schools disagreed about marriage law itself, and the Talmud says their families still married each other.
That's disagreement without hatred: the argument lasts, and so does the family table. Even when it's politics, the test is the same. Could you state the other side so well they'd nod?
Are you arguing with them, or only to win?

how: Jewish study runs on argument: the Talmud records the debates of the houses of Hillel and Shammai with both views kept, and Pirkei Avot holds them up as the model of an argument for the sake of heaven.

o: letting the most learned person settle the matter
arguing hard while still caring for the other person
agreeing to drop a topic so nobody gets upset

games.q: two kinds of argument — tap the pairs.
p: an argument for the sake of heaven

s: in Pirkei Avot, the good argument is the one that ends fast
an argument for the sake of heaven is the one that will last.
the law follows Hillel because his school argued better
the Talmud says because they were gentle and humble, and said Shammai's view first.
families from the two schools still married each other
even though they disagreed about marriage law, says the Talmud.

games.q: at a family dinner, your uncle and your mom disagree about a town vote. your uncle says: i'm right, so i don't need to hear her out. what would Hillel's students do?
o: hear her view in full, and even say it before their own.
if they were sure they were right, skip her side and move on.
change the subject; arguing at a family table is never for heaven.
games.why: the Talmud says Hillel's house taught Shammai's view and said it first. that humility, not winning, is why the law follows them.

practice: Choose one view you disagree with: a family rule, a team decision, a vote in your town. Say out loud, in a sentence or two, the best case for it, the way its smartest supporter would put it.
Then say quietly: that's their best case.

wordCard.voice: Disagreement without hatred: machloket l'shem shamayim, an argument for the sake of heaven, where you look for the truth and keep the person.

orig.note: Hebrew: an argument for the sake of heaven, the kind Pirkei Avot says will last.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: argue without hate. Hillel's students said the other side first, and the law went their way. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 5:17 (an argument for the sake of heaven will endure: Hillel and Shammai; one not for heaven: Korach and all his company)
Numbers 16 (Korach's revolt against Moses and Aaron)

Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (three years of dispute; 'these and these are the words of the living God'; the law follows Hillel's house because they were gentle and humble and cited Shammai's words first)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 14b (the two schools did not refrain from marrying each other's families)
